To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the structure and dynamics of fast ionic conductor β-alumina are investigated by classical molecular dynamics.
the Na ions occupy the Beevers–Ross site, that there is a tendency to form a vacancy in the conduction planes, and that the diffusion is close to Arrhenieuian in the temperature range 300–900K.
the structure of β-alumina can be described in a simple model that is in agreement with experiment and the dynamics of Na+ ions is consistent with experimental results.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the structure and dynamics of fast-ionic conductors.
the development of novel ionic conductors for electrochemical applications, in particular for the solid oxide fuel cell (SOFC), and the understanding of the fundamental processes involved.
the development of novel materials with improved performance for solid oxide fuel cells.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
our simulation results are consistent with the experimentally observed behaviour of β-alumina.
the Na+ ions are mobile in β-alumina, and that the mechanism of ionic conductivity in β-alumine is well understood.
the molecular dynamics simulation results are in good agreement with experiment for stoichiometric and non-stoichiometry β-alumina.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have found a mechanism for ionic conduction in Na+ β-alumina.
the A-site is the main site for ionic conduction, and the BR-site is the secondary site for conduction.
the structure of the Na+ ions in β-alumina can be described by an equilibrium between two types of sites: the aBR site and a site off-center in the conduction planes.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the A-site is not only a metastable state, but a thermodynamically stable position for Na+ ions.
aBR is the most stable Na+ site in stoichiometric Na+-β-aluma, while excess Na+ ions are stabilised by aBR shifts and BR vacancy creation.
the A-site occupation is a key factor for the ionic conduction in Na+β-alumina, and the interplay between the A-site, the BR-site and the BR-vacancies determines the ionic conductivity.
